Application of the Preferential Solvation Viscosity Model to Binary Liquid Mixtures: Aqueous, Nonaqueous, Ionic Liquid, and Deep Eutectic Solvent Systems

Alif Duereh,*,†,ID Yoshiyuki Sato,†,ID Richard Lee Smith, Jr.,*,†,‡,ID and Hiroshi Inomata† †Graduate School of Engineering, Research Center of Supercritical Fluid Technology, Tohoku University, Aramaki Aza Aoba 6-6-11, Aoba-ku, Sendai 980-8579, Japan ‡Graduate School of Environmental Studies, Research Center of Supercritical Fluid Technology, Tohoku University, Aramaki Aza Aoba 6-6-11, Aoba-ku, Sendai 980-8579, Japan

Supporting Information ABSTRACT: The preferential solvation (PS) viscosity model was used to correlate binary liquid viscosities of aqueous, nonaqueous, nonpolar–polar, molecular solvent–ionic liquid (IL), and molecular solvent–deep eutectic solvent mixtures for the purpose of determining local composition in the chemical systems and analysis of chemical phenomena. Lignin solubility in aqueous systems was directly proportional to the population of (1–2) complex molecules. Cellulose solubility in molecular solvent–IL mixtures was directly proportional to the population of (2–2) associated molecules. Local compositions determined from the PS viscosity model were able to be used to estimate mixture solvent polarity and the variation of carbazole selectivity in crude anthracene separations. Local compositions determined from the PS viscosity model can be used to analyze a wide variety of chemical phenomena in liquid solvent mixtures.

## 1. INTRODUCTION Binary liquid mixtures have many advantages over pure solvents in chemical reaction and separation processes. 1-3 For example, a properly chosen binary mixture of safe solvents can be used to replace hazardous solvents through methodologies based on physicochemical properties (e.g., Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameters 4-6 and Hansen solubility parameters 7). The bulk composition of a mixture of two solvents, "1" and "2" that have specific (1-2) molecular interactions is a convenient means to control selectivity or solvation effects in a reaction or separation. 8-10 However, the properties of binary liquid mixtures often show deviations from the mole fraction average of pure component liquid properties that are attributed to molecular interactions. Methods to quantify the specific molecular interactions in binary liquid mixtures are needed to allow one to take advantage of property changes that occur with bulk composition.

Viscosity is a key transport property that is needed to estimate fluid properties and mass transfer in chemical systems. Due to the complexity of molecular interactions, semitheoretical models such as Eyring theory¹¹ and free volume theory ¹²,¹³ are commonly applied to correlate liquid viscosities of binary mixtures. When low deviations in viscosity correlations are required for engineering design, modified Eyring viscosity models, McAllister, ¹⁴⁻¹⁶ Jouyban–Acree, ¹⁷,¹⁸ or Grunberg–

Nissan ^{19,20} models are used in which the adjustable parameters may be qualitatively related to the molecular features of a system. In previous work, ^{21} solvent exchange theory was used to develop a viscosity model based on preferential solvation (PS). The PS viscosity model allows the determination of local composition from bulk viscosity measurements and can be used to study variations in the population of (1–2) complex molecules or (1– 1) or (2–2) associated molecules.^{21}

Local composition of binary mixtures is generally accessible using spectroscopic techniques or molecular simulations; however, these approaches require detailed analyses and the specific interactions determined may not be directly related to the macroscopic property or the bulk composition. On the other hand, features of the hydration shell in aqueous mixtures or solvation shell in nonaqueous mixtures along with local composition can be quantified with the PS viscosity model through viscosity measurements.²¹

The PS viscosity model was compared with the McAllister, Jouyban– Acree, and Grunberg–Nissan viscosity models to explore parameter relationships. Local compositions obtained from the PS viscosity model were used to analyze several applications and to identify relationships between the local composition and the chemical phenomenon.

The objectives of this work were to (i) apply the preferential solvation viscosity model to correlate liquid viscosities of five types of molecular systems, (ii) analyze PS viscosity model parameters and their trends in molecular systems, (iii) examine relationships between PS viscosity model parameters with other viscosity model parameters, and (iv) examine four chemical applications related to cellulose solubility, lignin solubility, fractionation of carbazole from crude anthracene, and chromatographic mixed-solvent properties and analyze relation- ships between viscosity-derived local compositions and chemical phenomena in those applications.

## 3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION ### 3.1. Comparison of Viscosity Correlation Models. Table 1 provides a summary of correlation results for all viscosity models and for all molecular systems studied. In the discussion, the ideal liquid viscosity is defined as η^ideal^, which is the mole fraction average of the pure component viscosities at constant temperature and pressure. Table S1 (Supporting Information) provides a detailed list of the molecular systems and data sources^3,22,24–100^ and contains systems that exhibit viscosity maxima (+S), viscosity minima (–S) or positive (+), negative (–), or positive and negative (+–) deviations in mixture viscosity compared with η^ideal^. Parameter values shown in Table S1 for the PS viscosity model are discussed later. In Table 1, it can be seen that the PS, McAllister, and Jouyban–Acree models have relatively low (<2%) overall ARD, whereas the Grunberg–Nissan model has high (>7%) overall ARD. In comparing the PS viscosity model with other models, the PS viscosity model has lower ARD for aqueous systems and comparable ARD for the other molecular systems. All models provide low ARD (<1%) for nonpolar molecule–polar molecule systems.

Figure 1 shows typical results for correlation of selected binary mixtures (Figure 1a–e) for all viscosity models. The PS viscosity model conforms remarkably well to aqueous system data (Figure 1a) while the Grunberg–Nissan model provides a qualitative representation of systems that have a viscosity maximum (Figure 1a, b). All models provided reliable correlation of nonpolar–polar (Figure 1c), molecular solvent–IL (Figure 1d) and molecular solvent–DES (Figure 1e) mixtures, with the Jouyban–Acree model being able to conform most closely to the data than the other models.

Plots of the ARD in viscosity for all models versus composition for all systems are given in the Supporting Information (Figures S1–S4) along with parity plots (Figures S5–S8). In general, the PS viscosity model had the lowest ARD among the models examined for aqueous systems but higher ARD than the McAllister or Jouyban–Acree models for other molecular systems. The reason for the higher ARD of the PS viscosity model than the other models for molecular solvent–IL and molecular solvent–DES systems might be due to neglect of mutual (1–2) interactions (eq 7). The (1–2) interactions can be included in eq 5 to improve the correlation; however, this increases the number of parameters and reduces the reliability of their values according to the number of data. The PS model was compared with the other viscosity models using a minimal number of parameters, namely, eq 7 was used for molecular solvent–IL and molecular solvent–DES systems.

Analysis of the parameters of the PS model (Table S1) can provide some insight into the molecular interactions and the solution structure in the molecular systems. 21 For aqueous molecular systems (Table S1, nos. 1–14), when g$_{2/1}$ values are larger than unity, an S$_{2}$ molecule preferably

occupies the center of an arbitrary cybotactic region and is surrounded by S₁ (H₂O) molecules. Similarly, when g₁₂/₁ values are larger than unity, an S₁₂ (complex) molecule occupies the center of an arbitrary cybotactic region and is surrounded by S₁ (H₂O) molecules. For a given binary mixture among the aqueous molecular systems, the value of η₁₂ relative to the pure component η₁ or η₂ values indicate positive synergistic molecular interactions, because η₁₂ is greater than either the η₁ or η₂ values. All aqueous molecular systems shown have positive synergistic molecular interactions leading to viscosity maxima that are related to hydration shell formation. For aqueous mixtures of an HBA solvent, the size of the hydration shell around the S₁₂ complex molecules is proportional to the magnitude of the η₁₂ values.²¹ The presence of hydrophobic functional groups in a solute molecule increases the size of the hydration shell in aqueous mixtures,¹⁰¹ and correspondingly the values of η₁₂ and g₂/₁ for aqueous mixtures of methanol, ethanol, 1-propanol or 2-propanol in water (Table S1, nos. 11–14) tend to increase with the alcohol alkyl chain length.

For nonaqueous molecular systems (Table S1, nos. 15–53), some binary liquid mixtures have positive or negative synergistic molecular interactions, but most systems show negative deviations from ηideal. The strength of the interactions in nonaqueous molecular systems are generally weaker than those in aqueous molecular systems as evident by the relative size of the g2/1, g12/1 and η12 parameters compared with aqueous systems (Table S1), since a solvation shell, if it exists, contains loosely bound molecules.21,31 The g2/1 values in nonaqueous molecular systems (Table S1) are generally less than unity meaning that an S₁ molecule (methanol or ethanol) preferably occupies the center of an arbitrary cybotactic region and is surrounded by S₂ molecules. The η12 parameter values are generally less than or intermediate to the pure component viscosities, which indicates negative deviations from ηideal. Negative synergistic molecular interactions can be for methanol–dimethyl carbonate (Table S1, no. 23) and a number of ethanol–HBA molecular systems (Table S1, nos. 34–37, 41, 43, 48) in which complex molecule specific interactions are strong (high g12/1 values) and η12 values are less than either η₁ or η₂.

For nonpolar–polar molecular systems (Table S1, nos. 54– 77), self-association is the chief specific interaction (ij = 22) and all viscosity values had negative deviations from ηideal. In general, the g2/1 values were less than unity and the η22 values were intermediate to η₁ or η2, although there are a few exceptions (Table S1, nos. 54, 71, 73) due to the presence of a minimum in viscosity.

For molecular solvent-IL and molecular solvent-DES systems (Table S1, nos. 78-103), the solutions are made up of a low viscosity compound (1) and a high viscosity compound (IL or DES) such that the g2/1 values tend to be small indicating that the molecular solvent tends to be surrounded by the IL or DES. Based on the PS model parameters, the molecular solvent tends to occupy hydrophilic or hydrophobic free volume regions in the IL or DES framework. In general (Table S1), the η22 values are intermediate to η1 or η2 and the g22/1 values are larger than the g2/1 values implying that there is strong self-interaction of the IL or DES, thus justifying the use of eq 7.

The four-body interaction form of the McAllister model¹⁴ is required to describe systems with maxima in viscosity such as water–acetone or maxima and minima in viscosity such as methanol and toluene.¹⁰² The PS viscosity model can describe either maximum viscosity or minimum viscosity behavior well, and it can also describe both positive and negative deviations from ηⁱᵈᵉᵃˡ as evident by results for methanol–anisole, methanol–dichloromethane, and ethanol–chloroform in Table S1 (nos. 17, 21, 38). The PS viscosity model cannot describe molecular systems that have both a maximum and a minimum in mixture viscosity outside of the pure component viscosity values using only (1–2) or (2–2) interactions. However, by including additional terms (e.g., (1–2), (2–2), or both (1–2) and (2–1)), it may be possible to represent mixture viscosity of systems that have both a maximum and a minimum.

## 4.3. Chromatographic Analysis with Nonaqueous Molecular Systems. Mixtures of methanol and chloroform are typically used in chromatographic analyses 111,112 and for small-scale lipid extractions. 113 In some applications, a chloroform mole fraction of x2 = 0.2 is used 113 with the reason being related to solvent polarity (Figure 5a). 4.4. Cellulose Dissolution with Molecular Solvent–IL Systems. Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) can be added to 1-ethyl- 3-methylimidazolium diethyl phosphate ([EMIm][DEP]) ionic liquids to lower solution viscosity and to increase cellulose solubility (Figure 6a). 114 The phenomena is explained in the literature 114 by the increase in Kamlet–Taft basicity (β) of the solvent mixture (Figure 6b). Although (1-2), (2-2), and multibody interactions exist in molecular solvent-IL systems, the assumption of using only (2-2) self-interactions in the PS viscosity model to estimate local composition appears to be valid (Figure 7). Molecular simulations23 of molecular solvent-IL systems also show that the (2-2) self-interactions are much stronger than the (1-1) or (1-2) interactions in support of using only (2-2) self-interactions in eq 8. Agreement between PS viscosity-derived local compositions and spectral-derived local compositions (Figure 7) infers that the assumption of using (2-2) associated complexes in eq 8 can provide qualitative estimation of local composition trends in molecular solvent-IL mixture systems. In addition to molecular solvent-IL systems, the PS viscosity model is applicable to polymer solution-IL systems, in which viscosity-derived local compositions correlate with spectral-derived microviscosities115 for the polyethylene glycol (PEG)-[Bmim][PF6] system (Supporting Information, Figure S10).

## 5. CONCLUSIONS In this work, the preferential solvation (PS) viscosity model was used to correlate viscosities of five types of molecular systems, where it was found that the PS viscosity model gave lower deviations for aqueous systems than several commonly used viscosity models. The PS viscosity model was found to correlate liquid mixture viscosity data (2549 points) for five types of chemical systems to within an average relative deviation of 1.7%, compared with Grunberg–Nissan (7.6%), McAllister (1.6%), and Jouyban–Acree (1.7%) models. The PS viscosity model cannot describe chemical systems that have both a maximum and a minimum in viscosity with composition (methanol–toluene) using only (1–2) interactions so that it is likely that additional interactions are needed to describe such systems. The g₂/₁ and ηᵢⱼ parameters obtained from PS model are useful in analyzing the variation of viscosity with composition. Qualitative comparison of PS viscosity model parameters with pure component property viscosities allows one to readily recognize synergism in viscosity with composition, negative or positive deviations from ideal liquid viscosity, relative strength of

molecular interactions and relative size of hydration or solvation structures. Solubilities of lignin in solvent mixtures and solubilities of cellulose in solvent mixtures were found to be directly proportional to the population of (1–2) or (2–2) complexes, respectively, as determined from the PS viscosity model. The PS viscosity model is useful for explaining solvent mixture composition trends in example applications related to lignin solubility, carbazole separation, chromatographic analyses, and cellulose dissolution. The PS viscosity model is widely applicable to chemical systems and can be used to relate local composition effects to chemical phenomena.

Lignin solubility in aqueous systems was directly proportional to the population of (1–2) complex molecules. Cellulose solubility in molecular solvent–IL mixtures was directly proportional to the population of (2–2) associated molecules. Local compositions determined from the PS viscosity model were able to be used to estimate mixture solvent polarity and the variation of carbazole selectivity in crude anthracene separations. Local compositions determined from the PS viscosity model can be used to analyze a wide variety of chemical phenomena in liquid solvent mixtures. ## 1. INTRODUCTION Binary liquid mixtures have many advantages over pure solvents in chemical reaction and separation processes. 1-3 For example, a properly chosen binary mixture of safe solvents can be used to replace hazardous solvents through methodologies based on physicochemical properties (e.g., Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameters 4-6 and Hansen solubility parameters 7). The bulk composition of a mixture of two solvents, "1" and "2" that have specific (1-2) molecular interactions is a convenient means to control selectivity or solvation effects in a reaction or separation. 8-10 However, the properties of binary liquid mixtures often show deviations from the mole fraction average of pure component liquid properties that are attributed to molecular interactions. Methods to quantify the specific molecular interactions in binary liquid mixtures are needed to allow one to take advantage of property changes that occur with bulk composition. Viscosity is a key transport property that is needed to estimate fluid properties and mass transfer in chemical systems. Due to the complexity of molecular interactions, semitheoretical models such as Eyring theory¹¹ and free volume theory ¹²,¹³ are commonly applied to correlate liquid viscosities of binary mixtures. In previous work, ^{21} solvent exchange theory was used to develop a viscosity model based on preferential solvation (PS). VISCOSITY MODELS ### 2.1. Preferential Solvation Viscosity Model. The preferential solvation viscosity model assumes the existence of mutual (ij) complex molecules or (ii or jj) associated molecules formed from solvent i (Sᵢ) and solvent j (Sⱼ) due to the presence of strong specific molecular interactions, such as those resulting from hydrogen bond donor–acceptor functional groups. Solvation equations for several possible interactions are (Sᵢᴸ)m + mSⱼ ↔ᵍʲ/ⁱ (Sⱼᴸ)m + mSᵢ (1) $$(S^L_i)_m + \frac{m}{2}S_{ij} \overset{g_{ij}/i}{\rightleftharpoons} (S^L_{ij})_m + \frac{m}{2}S_i \quad (2)$$ (Sᵢᴸ)ₘ + m/2 Sⱼⱼ ↔ ᵍʲʲᐟⁱ (Sⱼⱼᴸ)ₘ + m/2 Sᵢ (3) The general form of the PS viscosity model is $$\eta_{\text{mix}} = \sum_{i=1}^N x_i^L \eta_i^0 + \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{j=i}^N x_{ij}^L \eta_{ij} \quad (4)$$ where, η_mix is the mixture viscosity, η_i^0 are the pure component (bulk) viscosities, N is the number of distinct molecular compounds, and the “L” superscript refers to the local composition of a solvent molecule. Subscripts denote a component _i_ or _j_ and a complex molecule subscript _ij_ = 12 or of an associated molecule (_ii_ = 11 or _jj_ = 22). For binary liquid mixtures, eq 4 becomes $\eta_{\text{mix}} = x_i^L \eta_i^0 + x_j^L \eta_j^0 + x_{ij}^L \eta_{ij} + x_{ii}^L \eta_{ii} + x_{jj}^L \eta_{jj}$ (5) Molecular interactions of the _ij_ type or of the _jj_ type are the main contribution to specific interactions in the five molecular systems of binary liquid mixtures studied. For aqueous solutions of a dipolar protophilic solvent (2) and for nonaqueous solutions of an HBD (1) and HBA (2) solvent, _eq_ 5 becomes $\eta_{\text{mix}} = x_1^{\text{L}}\eta_1^0 + x_2^{\text{L}}\eta_2^0 + x_{12}^{\text{L}}\eta_{12}$ (6) where $x^L_{12}$ is the local composition of the (12) complex molecule and $η_{12}$ is related to the viscosity of the (12) complex molecule. For solutions of nonpolar (1)–polar (2) molecules, the (2–2) self-interaction dominates the specific interactions in the molecular system, so that for nonpolar molecule–polar molecule solutions, eq 5 becomes $$\eta_{\text{mix}} = x_1^{\text{L}}\eta_1^0 + x_2^{\text{L}}\eta_2^0 + x_{22}^{\text{L}}\eta_{22} \quad (7)$$ Molecular solvent (1)–IL (2) and molecular solvent (1)–DES (2) systems have similar trends in viscosity as those for nonpolar (1)–polar (2) systems, because even though molecular solvent–IL systems have more than one type of specific interaction, (2–2) self-association of the ionic liquid is the chief specific interaction. 22,23 Similarly, for molecular solvent (1)–DES (2) systems, the (2–2) self-association of the DES is regarded to be the chief specific interaction in the molecular system, so that eq 7 is used in the analyses for both molecular solvent–IL and molecular solvent–DES systems. The main (i–j) interactions of five types of molecular systems are summarized in Table 1. The PS viscosity model is $\eta_{\text{mix}} = \eta_1 + \frac{g_{2/1}(\eta_2 - \eta_1)(x_2)^m + g_{ij/1}(\eta_{ij} - \eta_1)[(1 - x_2)x_2]^{m/2}}{(1 - x_2)^m + g_{2/1}(x_2)^m + g_{ij/1}[(1 - x_2)x_2]^{m/2}}$ (8) where g₂/₁, gᵢⱼ/₁, and ηᵢⱼ are preferential solvation parameters in which the average number of molecules (_m_) in a complex molecule (eqs 1, 2, and 8) is set equal to 2.5 according to results from previous work²¹ and based on preliminary assessment on five types of molecular systems studied in this work. Grunberg–Nissan Viscosity Model.** The Grunberg–Nissan viscosity model 19,20 is given by eq 12: ln(η_mix) = x_1ln(η_1) + x_2ln(η_2) + x_1x_2G_ij (12) where η_mix, η_1, and η_2 are the dynamic viscosities of the mixture, pure 1, and pure 2 components, respectively. The G_ij is a single adjustable binary interaction parameter related to the activation energy of molecular translation. ## 2.3. **McAllister Viscosity Model.** The four-body McAllister viscosity model^14^ was developed by considering the activation energy of molecular motion that can be expressed as the interaction of *ij* molecules given by *eq 13* ln(K_mix) = x_1^4 ln(K_1) + 4x_1^3 x_2 ln(K_1112) + 6x_1^2 x_2^2 ln(K_1122) + 4x_1 x_2^3 ln(K_2221) + x_2^4 ln(K_2) - ln[x_1 + x_2 M_2/M_1] + 4x_1^3 x_2 ln[(3 + M_2/M_1)/4] + 6x_1^2 x_2^2 ln[(1 + M_2/M_1)/2] + 4x_1 x_2^3 ln[(1 + 3M_2/M_1)/4] + x_2^4 ln[M_2/M_1] (13) where Kmix and the Ki parameters are the kinematic viscosity of the mixture and pure component i, respectively, and M is the molar mass. Equation 13 has three fitting parameters, K1112, K1122, and K2221 that are related to specific interactions in the molecular system. When eq 13 is applied to molecular solvent– DES mixtures, components 1 and 2 are defined to be the molecular solvent and the DES, respectively. 2.4. Jouyban–Acree Viscosity Model. The Jouyban– Acree model¹⁷ has three fitting parameters (A₀, A₁, A₂) and the following form: ln($\eta_{\text{mix}}$) = $x_1$ln($\eta_1$) + $x_2$ln($\eta_2$) + $A_0\left[\frac{x_1x_2}{T}\right]$ + $A_1\left[\frac{x_1x_2(x_1 - x_2)}{T}\right]$ + $A_2\left[\frac{x_1x_2(x_1 - x_2)^2}{T}\right]$ (14) ## 2.5. Analysis of the parameters of the PS model (Table S1) can provide some insight into the molecular interactions and the solution structure in the molecular systems. 21 For aqueous molecular systems (Table S1, nos. 1–14), when g$_{2/1}$ values are larger than unity, an S$_{2}$ molecule preferably occupies the center of an arbitrary cybotactic region and is surrounded by S₁ (H₂O) molecules. Similarly, when g₁₂/₁ values are larger than unity, an S₁₂ (complex) molecule occupies the center of an arbitrary cybotactic region and is surrounded by S₁ (H₂O) molecules. For a given binary mixture among the aqueous molecular systems, the value of η₁₂ relative to the pure component η₁ or η₂ values indicate positive synergistic molecular interactions, because η₁₂ is greater than either the η₁ or η₂ values. All aqueous molecular systems shown have positive synergistic molecular interactions leading to viscosity maxima that are related to hydration shell formation. For aqueous mixtures of an HBA solvent, the size of the hydration shell around the S₁₂ complex molecules is proportional to the magnitude of the η₁₂ values.²¹ The presence of hydrophobic functional groups in a solute molecule increases the size of the hydration shell in aqueous mixtures,¹⁰¹ and correspondingly the values of η₁₂ and g₂/₁ for aqueous mixtures of methanol, ethanol, 1-propanol or 2-propanol in water (Table S1, nos. 11–14) tend to increase with the alcohol alkyl chain length. For nonaqueous molecular systems (Table S1, nos. 15–53), some binary liquid mixtures have positive or negative synergistic molecular interactions, but most systems show negative deviations from ηideal. The strength of the interactions in nonaqueous molecular systems are generally weaker than those in aqueous molecular systems as evident by the relative size of the g2/1, g12/1 and η12 parameters compared with aqueous systems (Table S1), since a solvation shell, if it exists, contains loosely bound molecules.21,31 The g2/1 values in nonaqueous molecular systems (Table S1) are generally less than unity meaning that an S₁ molecule (methanol or ethanol) preferably occupies the center of an arbitrary cybotactic region and is surrounded by S₂ molecules. CONCLUSIONS In this work, the preferential solvation (PS) viscosity model was used to correlate viscosities of five types of molecular systems, where it was found that the PS viscosity model gave lower deviations for aqueous systems than several commonly used viscosity models. The PS viscosity model was found to correlate liquid mixture viscosity data (2549 points) for five types of chemical systems to within an average relative deviation of 1.7%, compared with Grunberg–Nissan (7.6%), McAllister (1.6%), and Jouyban–Acree (1.7%) models. The PS viscosity model cannot describe chemical systems that have both a maximum and a minimum in viscosity with composition (methanol–toluene) using only (1–2) interactions so that it is likely that additional interactions are needed to describe such systems. The g₂/₁ and ηᵢⱼ parameters obtained from PS model are useful in analyzing the variation of viscosity with composition. Qualitative comparison of PS viscosity model parameters with pure component property viscosities allows one to readily recognize synergism in viscosity with composition, negative or positive deviations from ideal liquid viscosity, relative strength of molecular interactions and relative size of hydration or solvation structures. Solubilities of lignin in solvent mixtures and solubilities of cellulose in solvent mixtures were found to be directly proportional to the population of (1–2) or (2–2) complexes, respectively, as determined from the PS viscosity model. The PS viscosity model is useful for explaining solvent mixture composition trends in example applications related to lignin solubility, carbazole separation, chromatographic analyses, and cellulose dissolution. The PS viscosity model is widely applicable to chemical systems and can be used to relate local composition effects to chemical phenomena. INTRODUCTION Binary liquid mixtures have many advantages over pure solvents in chemical reaction and separation processes. 1-3 For example, a properly chosen binary mixture of safe solvents can be used to replace hazardous solvents through methodologies based on physicochemical properties (e.g., Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameters 4-6 and Hansen solubility parameters 7). Methods to quantify the specific molecular interactions in binary liquid mixtures are needed to allow one to take advantage of property changes that occur with bulk composition. Viscosity is a key transport property that is needed to estimate fluid properties and mass transfer in chemical systems. VISCOSITY MODELS ### 2.1. Preferential Solvation Viscosity Model. The preferential solvation viscosity model assumes the existence of mutual (ij) complex molecules or (ii or jj) associated molecules formed from solvent i (Sᵢ) and solvent j (Sⱼ) due to the presence of strong specific molecular interactions, such as those resulting from hydrogen bond donor–acceptor functional groups. Solvation equations for several possible interactions are (Sᵢᴸ)m + mSⱼ ↔ᵍʲ/ⁱ (Sⱼᴸ)m + mSᵢ (1) $$(S^L_i)_m + \frac{m}{2}S_{ij} \overset{g_{ij}/i}{\rightleftharpoons} (S^L_{ij})_m + \frac{m}{2}S_i \quad (2)$$ (Sᵢᴸ)ₘ + m/2 Sⱼⱼ ↔ ᵍʲʲᐟⁱ (Sⱼⱼᴸ)ₘ + m/2 Sᵢ (3) The general form of the PS viscosity model is $$\eta_{\text{mix}} = \sum_{i=1}^N x_i^L \eta_i^0 + \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{j=i}^N x_{ij}^L \eta_{ij} \quad (4)$$ where, η_mix is the mixture viscosity, η_i^0 are the pure component (bulk) viscosities, N is the number of distinct molecular compounds, and the “L” superscript refers to the local composition of a solvent molecule. Subscripts denote a component _i_ or _j_ and a complex molecule subscript _ij_ = 12 or of an associated molecule (_ii_ = 11 or _jj_ = 22). For binary liquid mixtures, eq 4 becomes $\eta_{\text{mix}} = x_i^L \eta_i^0 + x_j^L \eta_j^0 + x_{ij}^L \eta_{ij} + x_{ii}^L \eta_{ii} + x_{jj}^L \eta_{jj}$ (5) Molecular interactions of the _ij_ type or of the _jj_ type are the main contribution to specific interactions in the five molecular systems of binary liquid mixtures studied. For aqueous solutions of a dipolar protophilic solvent (2) and for nonaqueous solutions of an HBD (1) and HBA (2) solvent, _eq_ 5 becomes $\eta_{\text{mix}} = x_1^{\text{L}}\eta_1^0 + x_2^{\text{L}}\eta_2^0 + x_{12}^{\text{L}}\eta_{12}$ (6) where $x^L_{12}$ is the local composition of the (12) complex molecule and $η_{12}$ is related to the viscosity of the (12) complex molecule. For solutions of nonpolar (1)–polar (2) molecules, the (2–2) self-interaction dominates the specific interactions in the molecular system, so that for nonpolar molecule–polar molecule solutions, eq 5 becomes $$\eta_{\text{mix}} = x_1^{\text{L}}\eta_1^0 + x_2^{\text{L}}\eta_2^0 + x_{22}^{\text{L}}\eta_{22} \quad (7)$$ Molecular solvent (1)–IL (2) and molecular solvent (1)–DES (2) systems have similar trends in viscosity as those for nonpolar (1)–polar (2) systems, because even though molecular solvent–IL systems have more than one type of specific interaction, (2–2) self-association of the ionic liquid is the chief specific interaction. 22,23 Similarly, for molecular solvent (1)–DES (2) systems, the (2–2) self-association of the DES is regarded to be the chief specific interaction in the molecular system, so that eq 7 is used in the analyses for both molecular solvent–IL and molecular solvent–DES systems. The main (i–j) interactions of five types of molecular systems are summarized in Table 1. The PS viscosity model is $\eta_{\text{mix}} = \eta_1 + \frac{g_{2/1}(\eta_2 - \eta_1)(x_2)^m + g_{ij/1}(\eta_{ij} - \eta_1)[(1 - x_2)x_2]^{m/2}}{(1 - x_2)^m + g_{2/1}(x_2)^m + g_{ij/1}[(1 - x_2)x_2]^{m/2}}$ (8) where g₂/₁, gᵢⱼ/₁, and ηᵢⱼ are preferential solvation parameters in which the average number of molecules (_m_) in a complex molecule (eqs 1, 2, and 8) is set equal to 2.5 according to results from previous work²¹ and based on preliminary assessment on five types of molecular systems studied in this work. Grunberg–Nissan Viscosity Model.** The Grunberg–Nissan viscosity model 19,20 is given by eq 12: ln(η_mix) = x_1ln(η_1) + x_2ln(η_2) + x_1x_2G_ij (12) where η_mix, η_1, and η_2 are the dynamic viscosities of the mixture, pure 1, and pure 2 components, respectively. The G_ij is a single adjustable binary interaction parameter related to the activation energy of molecular translation. ## 2.3. **McAllister Viscosity Model.** The four-body McAllister viscosity model^14^ was developed by considering the activation energy of molecular motion that can be expressed as the interaction of *ij* molecules given by *eq 13* ln(K_mix) = x_1^4 ln(K_1) + 4x_1^3 x_2 ln(K_1112) + 6x_1^2 x_2^2 ln(K_1122) + 4x_1 x_2^3 ln(K_2221) + x_2^4 ln(K_2) - ln[x_1 + x_2 M_2/M_1] + 4x_1^3 x_2 ln[(3 + M_2/M_1)/4] + 6x_1^2 x_2^2 ln[(1 + M_2/M_1)/2] + 4x_1 x_2^3 ln[(1 + 3M_2/M_1)/4] + x_2^4 ln[M_2/M_1] (13) where Kmix and the Ki parameters are the kinematic viscosity of the mixture and pure component i, respectively, and M is the molar mass. Equation 13 has three fitting parameters, K1112, K1122, and K2221 that are related to specific interactions in the molecular system. When eq 13 is applied to molecular solvent– DES mixtures, components 1 and 2 are defined to be the molecular solvent and the DES, respectively. 2.4. Jouyban–Acree Viscosity Model. The Jouyban– Acree model¹⁷ has three fitting parameters (A₀, A₁, A₂) and the following form: ln($\eta_{\text{mix}}$) = $x_1$ln($\eta_1$) + $x_2$ln($\eta_2$) + $A_0\left[\frac{x_1x_2}{T}\right]$ + $A_1\left[\frac{x_1x_2(x_1 - x_2)}{T}\right]$ + $A_2\left[\frac{x_1x_2(x_1 - x_2)^2}{T}\right]$ (14) ## 2.5. Analysis of the parameters of the PS model (Table S1) can provide some insight into the molecular interactions and the solution structure in the molecular systems. 21 For aqueous molecular systems (Table S1, nos. 1–14), when g$_{2/1}$ values are larger than unity, an S$_{2}$ molecule preferably occupies the center of an arbitrary cybotactic region and is surrounded by S₁ (H₂O) molecules. Similarly, when g₁₂/₁ values are larger than unity, an S₁₂ (complex) molecule occupies the center of an arbitrary cybotactic region and is surrounded by S₁ (H₂O) molecules. For a given binary mixture among the aqueous molecular systems, the value of η₁₂ relative to the pure component η₁ or η₂ values indicate positive synergistic molecular interactions, because η₁₂ is greater than either the η₁ or η₂ values. All aqueous molecular systems shown have positive synergistic molecular interactions leading to viscosity maxima that are related to hydration shell formation. For aqueous mixtures of an HBA solvent, the size of the hydration shell around the S₁₂ complex molecules is proportional to the magnitude of the η₁₂ values.²¹ The presence of hydrophobic functional groups in a solute molecule increases the size of the hydration shell in aqueous mixtures,¹⁰¹ and correspondingly the values of η₁₂ and g₂/₁ for aqueous mixtures of methanol, ethanol, 1-propanol or 2-propanol in water (Table S1, nos. 11–14) tend to increase with the alcohol alkyl chain length. For nonaqueous molecular systems (Table S1, nos. 15–53), some binary liquid mixtures have positive or negative synergistic molecular interactions, but most systems show negative deviations from ηideal. The strength of the interactions in nonaqueous molecular systems are generally weaker than those in aqueous molecular systems as evident by the relative size of the g2/1, g12/1 and η12 parameters compared with aqueous systems (Table S1), since a solvation shell, if it exists, contains loosely bound molecules.21,31 The g2/1 values in nonaqueous molecular systems (Table S1) are generally less than unity meaning that an S₁ molecule (methanol or ethanol) preferably occupies the center of an arbitrary cybotactic region and is surrounded by S₂ molecules. The η12 parameter values are generally less than or intermediate to the pure component viscosities, which indicates negative deviations from ηideal. CONCLUSIONS In this work, the preferential solvation (PS) viscosity model was used to correlate viscosities of five types of molecular systems, where it was found that the PS viscosity model gave lower deviations for aqueous systems than several commonly used viscosity models. The PS viscosity model was found to correlate liquid mixture viscosity data (2549 points) for five types of chemical systems to within an average relative deviation of 1.7%, compared with Grunberg–Nissan (7.6%), McAllister (1.6%), and Jouyban–Acree (1.7%) models. The PS viscosity model cannot describe chemical systems that have both a maximum and a minimum in viscosity with composition (methanol–toluene) using only (1–2) interactions so that it is likely that additional interactions are needed to describe such systems. The g₂/₁ and ηᵢⱼ parameters obtained from PS model are useful in analyzing the variation of viscosity with composition. Qualitative comparison of PS viscosity model parameters with pure component property viscosities allows one to readily recognize synergism in viscosity with composition, negative or positive deviations from ideal liquid viscosity, relative strength of molecular interactions and relative size of hydration or solvation structures. Solubilities of lignin in solvent mixtures and solubilities of cellulose in solvent mixtures were found to be directly proportional to the population of (1–2) or (2–2) complexes, respectively, as determined from the PS viscosity model. The PS viscosity model is useful for explaining solvent mixture composition trends in example applications related to lignin solubility, carbazole separation, chromatographic analyses, and cellulose dissolution. The PS viscosity model is widely applicable to chemical systems and can be used to relate local composition effects to chemical phenomena.
